paras: The killing of James Mason was the shooting of a Black man by a band of seven men at Dangerfield, Texas, on the night of August 1, 1895. The men called Mason out of his house and shot him dead, then fired into the house, wounding his wife, who was not expected to live, and one of his children. Papers outside Texas carried the news as a short wire item, one under the headline "Seven Texas Lynchers" and weekly digests attributing it to "whitecaps".

According to a dispatch from Dangerfield dated August 2, seven men came to Mason's home the previous night, called him out, and shot him dead. His wife escaped, ran into the house and got into bed with the children. The men then shot through a crack in the house, wounding her and one child. The dispatch said the child would recover but that the mother would die, and later digests described her as "fatally wounded".
None of the reports named the attackers, gave their race, or stated any accusation or motive against Mason.
No report of an inquest, arrests, or the wife's death appears in the coverage.

The news reached print on August 3 in papers far from Texas, all using the same brief wire text. The St. Paul Daily Globe headed it "SEVEN TEXAS LYNCHERS. Negro Shot Dead and His Wife and Child Wounded.", while the Wheeling Register called it "A MURDEROUS OUTRAGE." The Maysville Evening Bulletin ran the same text without a headline beneath a business report, and condensed versions appeared among miscellaneous news in the Evening Herald of Pennsylvania and the Wilmington Daily Republican and, on August 9, in the Marshall County Independent.

Weekly papers in Minnesota printing a "Summary of Week's News" reduced the episode to one line stating that "whitecaps shot and killed James Mason, a negro, and fatally wounded his wife." No Texas paper's account and no Black-press coverage of the killing was found.

reader.title: Killing of James Mason
bases: A band of seven men called a Black man out of his house at night and shot him dead, then shot his wife and child through the wall (A1, A2); a St. Paul headline called them 'lynchers' (A1) and news digests called them 'whitecaps' (A6, A7, A8).

Seven men acting with no stated authority killed James Mason (A1, A2), and the attackers were described as 'lynchers' (A1) and 'whitecaps' (A6); no accusation or motive is reported, so the pretext of justice or tradition is inferred from the night-band form rather than stated.
Every report, including the 'whitecaps' digests, traces to one Dangerfield wire dispatch of Aug. 2 (A1, A2, A6); no local Texas report, follow-up or Black-press account was found.

framing.detail: The Wheeling Register headed the dispatch 'A MURDEROUS OUTRAGE'.
The St. Paul Daily Globe headed it 'SEVEN TEXAS LYNCHERS. Negro Shot Dead and His Wife and Child Wounded.', naming the killing a lynching without comment.
Other papers ran the dispatch or a condensed version as an unheaded brief among other news.
Weekly digests in Minnesota papers reduced it to one line attributing the killing to 'whitecaps'.

conflicts.note: The Aug. 3 dateline in the Maysville paper is most likely a re-dating of the same wire text; the two papers carrying the Aug. 2 dateline are better evidence.
Not a contradiction: the digests add the label 'whitecaps', which the fuller dispatch does not use; its source is not shown.
